Mr. Speaker, sometimes some of us are accused of criticising schemes which are proposed and of not suggesting any alternative scheme. Of course, when we give an alternative scheme, somebody is sure to say that it is idealistic and impracticable, so we hesitate to do so; but I would suggest certain conditions which seem to me to be imperative if we are to have an immigration or colonization scheme upon which we can firmly base the future prosperity of this country.
First of all, I believe we should have free land for the intending immigrant. Some of the old-timers in this country boast of how they got on and how prosperous they became, and they are rather inclined to scoff at the newcomer because he does not do as well.
I would urge upon them this fact, that the earlier settlers in western Canada, and the same was true of eastern Canada, got

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
absolutely free Jand, and very frequently in comparatively accessible parts of the country. The newcomer to-day is not in as good a position as the immigrant who came into western Canada twenty or thirty or forty years ago.
Secondly, I would suggest that we must have cheap railroad rates.
Before the hon. member takes that up, I am sure he has something to offer that would be of considerable value in solving this problem of getting free land.

I will come to that in a moment.
The second condition that I would indicate would be the absolute necessity of cheap railroad rates. That has been emphasized in this House perhaps almost ad nauseam for many years, and yet we must get back to the fundamental fact that the railroads of Canada were built to serve the people of Canada, and yet under present conditions they are not serving them. We have the Canadian Pacific railway, a huge corporation, having drawn a great part of its capital from the people of this country in one form or another; we have this great Canadian National railway system which has been built up, and which is very heavily over-capitalized. Are these roads really filling the need? Remember that very few countries in the world are able to carry on successfully which are situated as our western country is, a thousand miles from the seaboard. The key to the situation is undoubtedly transportation.
The third condition I would lay down is cheap money-because under modern conditions the farmer, just as the business man, must do his business on credit. There is no use going back to the time of the pioneer settlers and suggesting that the settler to-day should do as the settler did thirty or forty years ago; he cannot.
The fourth condition I would urge is that in some way there must be a removal of the mortgages which so heavily bear upon industry to-day. We have the mortgages of the public debts; we have the mortgages created by inflated land values; we have the mortgages created by watered stock; we have mortgages of all kinds, which are very largely responsible for the high cost of production at 9 p.m. the present time. When we say, do away with these things, immediately there is an outcry. Free land? The land is held by speculators and corporations, a considerable amount of it, and they refuse to relinquish it from their grasp. The colonization scheme that was brought to this

We speak of cheap railroad rates, and immediately we are up against these railroad corporations, and particularly that corporation of which the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) spoke the other night. We speak of cheap money; those of us who were in the last parliament know the difficulties we had in the Banking and Commerce committee when we spoke of any means by which cheaper money could be obtained for the farmers. And as to the removal of mortgages, even any modest suggestion that we could reduce our public debt or force the overcapitalized industries to let out a little of the water is immediately met by an outcry. And so the great mass of the people of this country are coming more and more clearly to recognize that the policies of Canada, the fundamental policies, have been in the past dictated to no small extent by a comparatively small group of financiers. I do not know just what the outcome is going to be. I have sometimes hoped that in the shake-up we get in this parliament a definite line of demarcation may foe established between those who represent the big interests and those who represent the interests of the common people of this country. The trouble is that in dealing with the immigration question we have looked at the matter altogether too much from the standpoint of immigration companies, or from the standpoint of trade returns, or through official eyes, and not sufficiently from the Standpoint of the local community or of the immigrant himself. I would urge that we take a great deal more care in the very difficult and very delicate process of transplanting human beings from one country to another, or from one environment to another. We all know how, in the spring time, we sometimes transplant tomato plants or cabbage plants from window-boxes out into the open, and we then take a great deal of care to set up a can, a shingle, or something of that kind, to shelter the tender plants from the hot sun or from the wind. What do we do in the case of human beings coming to Canada? Why we wheelbarrow them into this country, dump them, and leave them to shift for themselves as best they can. We recall the saying that "To teach puppies to swim, chuck them in." Apparently we have acted on that

theory, and while some of the puppies have managed to swim, others have gone to the bottom. In any case there has been an immense amount of hardship, and we have been loaded up with problems in this country that it will take years to solve. May I give an illustration? I found that a very considerable portion of the stock was low grade stock. The people frequently were growing crops from comparatively poor seed. Somebody put it to me rather graphically in speaking of the conditions away out north of Edmonton, when he said that you could' almost tell how far away you were from the city by the size of the hogs-they were so much better a breed and would pay so much better when they were adjacent to civilization, or where .there were facilities for carrying on stock raising scientifically. I found out that there were a very large number of women at that time who were very much isolated, and the same thing is true to this day. I know that a very considerable number of women inmates of the North Battleford Insane Hospital were afflicted with melancholia induced by the hardships and isolation which they had to endure. I found there was a very considerable lack of education in many districts. I do not give these

as general conditions, but I know they prevail in many of the backward parts of this country, the very parts to which we are sending immigrants. I may say that I called the attention of the then Premier of Saskatchewan to these facts, and I brought to him a scheme by which we could do something to remedy these evils, by placing demonstration farms within easy access of those districts, having consolidated schools, district nurses, and so on. I should like to refer very briefly not merely to the material needs of the immigrants, which ought to be attended to if we are to evolve any thorough-going scheme of immigration, but also to their cultural needs. There are two rules that I should like to lay down in this connection. They have come to me after some years of experience with these immigrant peoples, and they are practical rules. The first is, that we should give to these people the best that we have, and the second is that we should take from them the best that they bring. Let me pause to develop very briefly my thought. Sometimes I should like to write an article on "How the foreigner sees Canada," as he arrives in this country by the railroads, as he stops at the immigration hall, as he passes out into our little towns, as he goes into the cheap hotels or lodging houses; as his daughters go into the restaurant kitchens, as they attend the cheap movie shows. Do we ever consider what Canada looks like through the eyes of a foreigner? We have given them the very roughest and hardest side of Canadian life. Many of them have been here for years, yet they know nothing of the history, traditions, or cultural life of this country. Sometimes we find the results in the police court when boys or girls who have run wild are brought before the magistrate, and then we have the task of sending them to the reformatory or attempting to punish them. Perhaps we ought rather to

adopt the attitude which is said to be that of the Chinese educationist, who, when somebody goe3 wrong, punishes the parents and guardians and not the children. The fact is that in a great many of these cases it is we who are to blame and not the foreigners who have come to our midst. It may be true that the foreigner comes here with a small percentage of assets in money, but I submit he brings with him cultural assets that are by no means negligible. We have people coming to us from all parts of the European continent who seem to be bom with an innate love of music and with an ability to express themselves through music. I think I might say: God forbid! We in this country have not so far attained such a standard of beauty or goodness that we want all the people to be made in our own image. We forget sometimes that in the effort to make these people like us we drive out of them the very highest things which they bring to us.
Again, let me given an illustration which came under my notice a few years ago. The then Governor General, Earl Grey I think, was visiting the schools of the city of Winnipeg, and he was told that a large number of the children were of foreign extraction. So His Excellency asked all the Ukrainian children to hold up their hands. Not a hand went up. Then he asked for a show of hands from all the German children, and not a hand went up. It was the same in the case of Polish children-no move. His

The fact is that those children have been so taught that they are ashamed of their origin, and a man that is ashamed of his origin is not worth having in this country. What would you think of an Englishman or a Scotchman who would throw off his nationality and culture just as a man throws off his coat? We have not thought seriously enough of this question. We have brought these immigrants here to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, and if we are able to work them more cheaply than Canadians, we are anxious to bring them in by the shipload. What is called patriotism is taught in this country, but we should think a little more of what patriotism involves.

I will just say that that is a very common, I would go almost as far as to say a prevalent attitude throughout the greater part of western Canada.

The result has been that very frequently, in the course of a few years, we have little isolated foreign colonies throughout the country. Those who are desirous of promoting Canadian unity very often say that this state of things should not

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
exist and that we should mix the people all together. They cannot possibly have their church, halls, schools, cooperative societies and all that kind of thing to which they have been accustomed in the Old Land. that land. The metal used in the manufacture of big German guns which bombarded Paris from a distance of twenty miles during the war was said to be nickel steel. So that nickel became of value for armaments, but as hon. members will very well remember, in the month of February, 1922, at the Washington armament conference, the nickel industry over night lost seventy per cent of its market. Thus the nickel industry in one day received a blow from which it has not yet recovered. It had at that time reached its highest state of development; it was producing 85 per cent of the world's supply. Up until 1920 two large corporations, engaged in the mining of this valuable mineral, the International Nickel Corporation of Sudbury, and the Mond Nickel Company at Copper Cliff, had been supplying the needs of the world. In 1917 or 1918 the British American Nickel Company was organized, but as a result of the circumstances which have been referred on a few occasions during this debate, it operated for only one year. During its operation the price of nickel dropped from 33 and 32 cents to 23 cents a pound. Owing to the decision of the Washington disarmament conference to discontinue the building of dreadnoughts and battleships, the International Nickel Company closed their plant, and it remained closed for fully a year and a half; but during this time the Nickel Corporation did not remain idle. At the cost of a very large sum of money, and by the aid of scientific research in an attempt to reduce the price to the consumer, they evolved a new method of producing nickel at a very much smaller cost than was possible in pre-war times. The Nickel Corporation, after two years of research and expending large sums of money, were able, not only to evolve this new process, but to develop new uses for nickel. To-day nickel is used in the manufacture of aeroplanes, in the manufacture on a small scale of automobiles; it is sold in rods, bars and ingots, as an alloy in making tools, and especially in making pipe, utensils and so forth-products which are affected by acids- because nickel has the quality of resisting the effects of acid. It was only after this prolonged research and a great expenditure of money that the nickel industry achieved anything like the success it had had in pre-war times. As I said before, the International Nickel Company is producing metal at the present time, and this metal is now sold to the steel industry in the United States.

The metal as it leaves the refinery now is in the final state in which it is sold, so far as the International Nickel Company is concerned. Nickel in the markets of the world to-day is an article that is sold exactly like copper. The International Nickel Company has developed in Canada what is to-day one of the key industries of the world, and that has been done without assistance from either this government or the provincial government. This industry has developed the entire Sudbury district, and has made possible also the development of large areas of agricultural lands which depend, in large measure, upon the nickel industry for existence.

I did not intend to speak about the tariff in my speech on the Address, but a great deal has been said about the tariff. The tariff, I believe, is one of the questions upon which the next election will be fought and upon which my hon. friends on the opposite side of the House will again meet the electorate of Canada. The way in which the tariff has been discussed, the way in which it is understood by the mass of consumers, is a great misrepresentation of conditions as they exist. It has been Said by some of our friends opposite that the tariff is a tax. It has even been said by some of them that there is a great distinction between a tariff and protection. The point I wish to make is that whether it is protection or whether it is a tariff, during the last campaign our hon. friends opposite appealed to the people of Canada for a higher tariff, for a tariff such as they had before. Throughout the country, in the press, on every platform, the arguments used by our opponents were

The Address-Mr. Lapierre

that conditions in Canada were such as they are owing to the fact that we had reduced the tariff; that a high tariff or a higher tariff would bring greater prosperity to the country. It has been admitted by speakers on the opposite side of the House that conditions in Canada are far better to-day than they were in 1901 when this govemmemt came into power. It has also been admitted that our trade balance is very much more favourable to-day than it was then. I have in my hand the Dominion Bureau of Statistics returns of Canadian exports and imports by groups. In 1920 our unfavourable trade balance was $34,115,907, and as all our hon. friends remember, at that period- our currency was greatly depreciated. Our Canadian dollar was at that time worth 87 or 88 cents in the monetary markets of the world. But in 1922, one year after this government came into power, our favourable trade balance was $135,768,542, and in 1925, it amounted to $392,831,447. These results were obtained while we were being accused of reducing the tariff. Our hon. friends opposite at that -time were telling the consuming public and the great mass of the producers that Canada's best market was the home market, and at that very moment in the United- States they were appealing to the American people along the same lines. What has been the result of the Fordney-McCum-ber tariff in the United States? Shortly after the advent of the Coolidge administration, the President of the United States named a commission to inquire into agricultural conditions in .the western states, and soon after the report was made, Mr. Herbert Hoover in a statement made to the Board of Trade of the city of New York stated that, in view of this report, the United States had- reached a stage where they had become a self-contained nation, a nation producing for its home consumption and consuming its own production, and that owing to the high cost of production in that country, the United States farmer could no longer expect to export his surplus to the markets of the world. He advised the farmers of the United States to reduce their production to the requirements of the United States market. This has been intensified during the last three or four months, and we find that in the four agricultural states, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and Dakota there is a great movement against the Coolidge government on account of its attitude towards a high tariff. They have realized that no nation can be prosperous when agriculture is not prosperous. I have before me an extract from an American periodical in which conditions which now exist in those western states is

very plainly set forth. In a despatch to the New York Tribune by Mark Sullivan, I read the following:
The east, either through preoccupation with its own prosperity or for whatever reasons may be, failed to know what was happening among the farmers. At a moment when values of corporations were mounting on the New York Stock Exchange the value of land was going downward. When manufacturing corporations were announcing stock dividends and eastern banks announcing record earnings, western banks and other institutions were embarrassed, in many cases to the point of failure, by the decline in values of farm land, farm mortgages, and some farm crops.
Now that Washington's attention has been called to it forcibly, the contrast between east and west is almost dramatic. The western condition includes an average of more than two bank failures a day; sheriffs' sales in nearly every county seat; cuts in the rents of city houses and apartments of as much as 50 per cent; an estimate by the Nebraska State Bureau of Crop Statistics that the purchasing power of the farmers has suffered a reduction of $62,000,000 this year.
This condition gives rise to a political mood just beginning to express itself in attacks on the tariff, on the railroads, whose earnings and values go up as the farmers' go down; on the federal reserve system, and on 'big business.' It is in some degree similar to the condition which arose in the middle of President Taft's term, and which expresssed itself in the election of a Democratic Congress and in Roosevelt's attempt to prevent Taft's renomination.
The farmer's situation presents the greatest, most far-reaching and most perilous economic problem with which the American people are faced, declares B. F. Yoakum, Chairman of the Board of the Frisco railroad system and a recognized authority on the farmer's problems. According to Mr. Yoakum, the American farmer is in a worsj situation to-day than at any time in his history.
Representative L. J. Dickinson of Iowa has introduced a bill in Congress to provide for the disposal, through co-operative and pivate agencies, of the surplus of wheat, corn, rice, cotton, tobacco, cattle and swine. And Senator Capper, a Kansas representative who owns twelve or thirteen profitable farm papers, and who is said to be particularly quick and sure in detecting the drift of public sentiment in his state, has suggested a retaliatory campaign against manufacturers because of the failure of the farmers to obtain what they have demanded of Congress. If this is the result of the operation of a high protective tariff in the United States, which is practically a self-sustaining country, what would be the result of a tariff such as our friends opposite suggest should be put into force in this country? Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that they are in favour of a tariff such as they have in the United States, and I find that during the last campaign the leader of the opposition expressed himself in very definite terms on this subject. I shall ask the House to listen to various statements he made in different places.

Canada is a wonderful country, and I sometimes think that instead of the doleful remarks depreciating different parts of Canada, if we devoted more time to publishing to the world the greatness of our resources it would be far better for our constituencies in particular and the Dominion as a whole. The late iMark Twain tells a story of a visit which he once made to Mount Vesuvius. As he looked with wonder and astonishment on that great work of nature a native came up to him and said, "You have nothing in your country, Sir, that can touch that." Mark Twain turned to him and with pride and indignation swelling his breast he said, "We have a waterfall in our country, Sir, that would put that thing out of business in five minutes." And so it is with everything that we have in the Dominion. Canada has the greatest wheat fields; Canada has the greatest coal fields; Canada has the greatest gold fields; Canada has the most varied distribution of precious and economic minerals; Canada has the most extensive forests; Canada has the most extensive fisheries; Canada has the greatest number of miles of river and lake navigation; Canada has the greatest extent of coast line, and Canada has the greatest area of pasturage and arable lands of any country in the world.
